item.title: Beyond 3SUM-Hardness for Geometric Problems
item.description: arXiv:2610.32162v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Since the early days of fine-grained complexity, many geometric problems have been shown to require quadratic time under the 3SUM Hypothesis. But as the 3SUM Hypothesis was recently refuted, these lower bounds have lost their foundation. In this note we point out that many of them can be recovered under an alternative hardness assumption, the $k$-AP Hypothesis. The required changes to the proofs are trivial, so the lower bounds remain just as easy to teach.
item.dc:creator: Nick Fischer

item.title: The Exact Robustness of Smith's Rule with Predicted Processing Times
item.description: arXiv:2610.32197v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Smith's rule orders jobs by their weight-to-processing-time ratios. We study the robustness of its list schedule on identical parallel machines when job $j$ is ordered using a nominal processing time $\mu_j$ and its true processing time satisfies $\mu_j\leq p_j\leq\alpha\mu_j$, where $\alpha\geq1$. We determine the exact worst-case approximation ratio against the clairvoyant optimum, taking the supremum over machine counts. The ratio is an explicit continuous piecewise-algebraic function of $\alpha$. It equals the Kawaguchi--Kyan constant $(1+\sqrt{2})/2$ at $\alpha=1$ and is exactly $\sqrt{\alpha}$ for $\alpha\geq4$. On one machine the exact ratio is $\sqrt{\alpha}$. For every fixed machine count, no deterministic nonpreemptive algorithm can improve on this guarantee, even with knowledge of $\alpha$. The proof reduces to a common nominal Smith ratio and endpoint errors. Cutting the list schedule at its minimum final machine load yields a prefix--suffix certificate; two packings of matching lower-bound instances explain the branches below $\alpha=4$. We also prove a nominal-to-robust transfer: any fixed schedule ordered by nominal Smith ratios on each machine, with nominal approximation ratio $1+\delta$, has realized ratio at most $\sqrt{\alpha}+\alpha\delta$. A nominal approximation scheme then gives, for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$, a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm independent of $\alpha$ with ratio $(1+\varepsilon)\sqrt{\alpha}$ simultaneously for $1\leq\alpha\leq4$.
item.dc:creator: Ohad Ayalon, Ilan Reuven Cohen

item.title: Exact Algorithms and Complexity of the Smallest Grammar Problem
item.description: arXiv:2610.32298v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Smallest Grammar Problem (SGP) asks for a smallest straight-line grammar generating a given string, where size is the total length of the right-hand sides. Rules may be nested, so locally optimal choices of repeated fragments need not combine into an optimal grammar. We show that in an optimal grammar one can choose an occurrence of the expansion of each auxiliary nonterminal such that these intervals are pairwise disjoint. Hence the dictionary can be read off from a partition of the input, decoupling the choice of the dictionary from the parsing of rules. Using this property together with a bound on references to rules of length two, we obtain an exact algorithm running in $O^*(1.8723^n)$ time and $O(n)$ words of space, improving the $O^*(3^n)$ bound of Casel et al. for general grammars. For alphabet size $\sigma$ and $R=\log_\sigma n$, we give a $2^{O((n/R)\log(R+1))}$-time algorithm, which is subexponential for fixed alphabets. Conversely, using an anchor-based projection from encoded grammars back to source grammars, we prove that SGP is NP-complete over a binary alphabet, answering a question of Casel et al., and construct instance families of tunable alphabet size on which no $2^{o(n/R)}n^{O(1)}$-time algorithm exists under ETH. Finally, for every $c>1$ we give a constant-degree integer polynomial formulation of SGP with $O(c^n)$ variables. By the barrier theorem of Belova, Golovnev, Kulikov, Mihajlin, and Sharipov, a proof that SGP is $\lambda^n$-SETH-hard under their deterministic fine-grained reductions would imply new lower bounds for Boolean series-parallel circuits or for arithmetic circuits.
item.dc:creator: Xiangle Chen

item.title: Tightening the Online Bin Packing Gap from Both Sides, and the Limits of the Current Methods
item.description: arXiv:2610.32367v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The asymptotic competitive ratio of online bin packing has been bracketed since 2018 by the lower bound 1.54278 of Balogh, Bekesi, Dosa, Epstein and Levin and the upper bound 1.57829 of their Advanced Harmonic algorithm. We revisit both sides with exact rational computation and prove what the computations say. On the upper bound, we rebuild the certification of Advanced Harmonic as an exact optimization over its dual parameters; with the published parameters this already certifies a ratio strictly below the published one, and re-tuning the algorithm's proportion parameters gives a certified ratio of 1.5782147437 (an exact rational), independently re-verified on all 402 scenarios. To our knowledge this is the first movement of the upper bound since 2018. On the lower bound, we prove that the 2018 adversary construction is rigid: extending it by any finite number of new batches of ordinary size (outside the window of sizes s with 2s > 1 and rational part at most 0.64819), placed anywhere, with counts depending on the observed statistics, adaptive or not, never improves the bound at any truncation level. The load-bearing fact is that the construction is volume-tight at every stop. A single window-sized batch added to the truncation-3 tree is shown by machine-verified certificates to leave its value below the published limit. A computational map covers the remaining natural extensions: unions of structural variants, two-statistic multi-batch adversaries, and three families of adaptive conditions that the paper's separation theorem allows but never uses; none improves the bound. On the algorithm side we show that the marking, bonus-item and red-sand mechanisms of Extreme Harmonic bind nowhere in Advanced Harmonic, whose bottleneck is a two-medium-item bin that no known mechanism targets. We record two corrections to commonly cited numbers.
item.dc:creator: Karyamsetty Martin

item.title: Pareto-optimal Scheduling with Predictions
item.description: arXiv:2610.32503v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study preemptive single-machine scheduling with predictions, where a prediction of the order of the jobs (or of their sizes) is available, and the objective is to minimize the total completion time. An algorithm is $c$-consistent if it is $c$-competitive when the prediction is correct, and $R$-robust if it is $R$-competitive whatever the prediction. Since the introduction of this problem as one of the first examples of learning-augmented algorithms, the best possible trade-off between consistency and robustness has remained open. We determine it exactly for deterministic algorithms. For every $R>2$, we give an $R$-robust algorithm whose consistency is \[ c(R)=R\Big(1-\Big(1-\frac{R+2}{R^2}\Big)^{\frac R{R+2}}\Big), \] and we prove that no deterministic $R$-robust algorithm, with either predicted order or predicted job sizes, has better consistency. In particular, consistency $1+\eps$ is achievable with robustness $\eps^{-1/2}+\frac16+O(\sqrt\eps)$, whereas all previous algorithms required robustness $\Theta(1/\eps)$. Our algorithm is greedy: it follows the predicted order as fast as possible, subject to the invariant that the cost paid so far is at most $R$ times the optimum of the instance in which every unfinished job would end immediately. The matching lower bound rests on the observation that every robust deterministic algorithm must satisfy the same invariant along its run on correct predictions.
item.dc:creator: Ziyad Benomar, Vianney Perchet

item.title: Single-Machine Guarantees on Unrelated Machines and Beyond: Proportional Fairness for Nonclairvoyant Polytope Scheduling
item.description: arXiv:2610.32545v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Polytope Scheduling Problem (PSP) is a general framework for preemptive scheduling in which feasible instantaneous job allocations form a packing polytope. In the nonclairvoyant online setting, Proportional Fairness (PF), a practical allocation rule rooted in market theory, is the leading general-purpose algorithm. On a single machine, PF coincides with weighted Round-Robin, which is $2$-competitive for weighted completion time with uniform release dates (optimal for nonclairvoyant algorithms) and $(2+\varepsilon)$-speed $O(1/\varepsilon)$-competitive for weighted flow time. Known guarantees beyond a single machine are weaker. This raises a central question: Are these heterogeneous environments intrinsically harder than a single machine under nonclairvoyance? We show that they are not: PF retains both single-machine guarantees on the novel class of support-submodular polytopes, which includes unrelated machines and polymatroids. On unrelated machines, this refutes a belief (JACM'18, SODA'25) that PF is not $O(1)$-speed $O(1)$-competitive for weighted flow time. Our main technical contribution is an equivalent characterization: a polytope is support submodular if and only if, for all job weights, the optimal weighted completion time is concave in the processing requirements. This structural insight underlies both guarantees. For general PSP, the picture changes: we give the first lower bound above $2$, showing that every randomized nonclairvoyant algorithm has a competitive ratio of at least $2+10^{-5}$ for weighted completion time, even with uniform release dates. On the positive side, we substantially improve the best known guarantee for weighted completion time from $27$ (SICOMP'26) to $4$ via a new dual-fitting analysis of PF. For weighted flow time, we show that PF achieves the first $O(1)$-speed $O(1)$-competitive nonclairvoyant guarantee for graph scheduling.
item.dc:creator: Alexander Lindermayr, Sven J\"ager, Bart Zondervan

item.title: Combinatorial Minimum Cost Flow in Almost-Linear Time on Dense Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.32556v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a combinatorial algorithm that computes an exact minimum-cost flow in $n^{2+o(1)}$ time. This is the first combinatorial improvement since Goldberg-Tarjan [GT87], and is almost optimal in dense graphs. All previous faster algorithms, including the almost-linear-time algorithm of Chen et al. [CKL+22], rely on interior-point methods. Our main conceptual contribution is a black-box reduction from exact minimum-cost flow on general graphs to its approximation on DAGs, with only an $n^{o(1)}$ loss on the running time. This reduction allows future work on combinatorial minimum-cost flow to focus on DAGs, typically much easier to handle than general graphs. Our $n^{2+o(1)}$-time algorithm follows by combining this reduction with a simple augmenting-path-based approximation algorithm on DAGs. The reduction is based on a new structural result, called a flow-cost-preserving DAG projection. Given an arbitrary directed graph, this construction produces a DAG that approximately preserves both the congestion of flows and their cost up to a small loss.
item.dc:creator: Bernhard Haeupler, Yonggang Jiang, Thatchaphol Saranurak

item.title: A Linear Lower Bound for Convex Body Chasing in Every $\ell_p$ Norm
item.description: arXiv:2610.32670v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish an $\Omega(d)$ lower bound on the competitive ratio of convex body chasing in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with $\ell_p$ movement costs for any $p \in [1, \infty)$. Previously, the best known lower bound for general $p$ was $\Omega(\max\{\sqrt{d}, d^{1-1/p}\})$, established by Bubeck et al. (2019); a linear lower bound was known only for $p = \infty$, realized by the standard construction of chasing faces of a hypercube. Our lower bound strictly improves on the prior bound for every fixed $p \in [1, \infty)$ and shows that the functional Steiner point algorithm of Sellke (2023) - which has competitive ratio $O(d)$ - is asymptotically optimal for every $\ell_p$ norm. Our lower bound is based on the recursive construction of Bubeck, Coester, and Rabani (2023) for metrical service systems, which gives a lower bound of $\Omega(r^2)$ for requests of size $O(r)$ in that setting. We show that requests in their construction, each comprising a set of discrete points in a graph metric, can be mapped to the vertices of convex requests in a $(2r+1)$-dimensional vector space while approximately preserving movement costs up to a factor of $O(r)$, which establishes the lower bound.
item.dc:creator: Nicolas Christianson

item.title: Deterministic Incremental Triconnectivity in $O(\log^2 n)$ Worst-Case Time
item.description: arXiv:2610.32721v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the problem of maintaining the triconnectivity in some biconnected graph G in the incremental dynamic setting. We consider updates in the form of edge insertions and edge subdivisions, and triconnectivity queries, i.e. queries of the form "are there at least three vertex disjoint paths between a and b?". All algorithms presented in this paper are deterministic. All queries and updates are answered in worst-case $O(\log n)$ time. By combining this result for biconnected graphs with a result of Holm and Rotenberg [SODA'20] we get an algorithm for general graphs with a worst-case running time of $O(\log^2 n)$ per operation. These algorithms represent an improvement of the state-of-the-art by a factor of $O(\log n)$.
item.dc:creator: Niels Inselmann Christiansen, Eva Rotenberg

item.title: Selection under partial information
item.description: arXiv:2610.32731v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The selection problem asks to find the $k$-th smallest element in a given set $X$. Its complexity is well-known to be $\Theta(|X|)$ for every fixed $k$. We consider the poset selection problem where a partial order $P$ on $X$ is given, and the underlying order of $X$ is guaranteed to be a linear extension of $P$. This generalizes several variants of the selection problem studied before. Our main result is an algorithm that performs $O( k + \operatorname{OPT}(P,k) )$ comparisons, where $\operatorname{OPT}(P,k)$ is the minimum number of comparisons required for the input $(P,k)$. If $P$ is a rooted tree, we obtain an $O( \operatorname{OPT} \log (k / \operatorname{OPT}) )$ algorithm, which can be further improved to $O( \operatorname{OPT} \log \log (k/\operatorname{OPT}) )$ or $O( \operatorname{OPT} \log \operatorname{OPT})$ under mild assumptions about $P$. Our algorithms are based on the work of Kaplan, Kozma, Zamir, and Zwick [SOSA 2019], who used Chazelle's soft heaps [J. ACM 2000] to simplify several older results. We introduce a new soft heap variant, the weighted soft heap, which allows greater control over which elements get corrupted.
item.dc:creator: Benjamin Aram Berendsohn

item.title: Structure and Exact Certification of Nonnegative Tensor Decompositions
item.description: arXiv:2610.32787v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the structure and exact certification of nonnegative tensor decompositions supplied through rational factor matrices. Every failure of minimality or essential uniqueness contains an irreducible positive exchange between $p$ supplied terms and $q$ competing terms. A dimension count based on the Lovitz--Petrov splitting theorem bounds the effective order of such an exchange, the sum over the modes of the joint factor-span dimension minus one, by $p+q-2$, and this bound is attained at every supplied length $R\ge2$. After eliminating ambient-row variables by the Farkas lemma, the resulting semialgebraic systems have fewer than $2R^2$ real variables. For input bit length $L$, this gives a deterministic $G(R)L^{O(R^2)}$-time algorithm that computes the nonnegative rank and an exact minimum-length decomposition, decides minimality and essential uniqueness, and returns exact witnesses when either property fails. The exponent is independent of the tensor order and the mode dimensions. For Lebesgue moment tensors, positive quadrature determines the nonnegative rank and the uniqueness behavior, and some rational length-$R$ inputs force a common field of degree at least $\lfloor R/2\rfloor!$ for any exact minimum-length output. As an illustration, an implementation resolves all 114 instances left inconclusive by earlier positive-scattering criteria, of which 95 are minimal and essentially unique and 19 are minimal but nonunique.
item.dc:creator: Haoming Wang, Ming Yuan

item.title: Compressed Boolean Matrix Multiplication using Bicliques
item.description: arXiv:2610.32836v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Boolean matrix multiplication is a fundamental operation in many graph-based applications, including web and social network analysis, information retrieval, and graph query evaluation. However, conventional sparse representations such as CSR}/CSC still incur significant space and time costs on large graphs. In this work, we introduce a method for multiplying Boolean matrices based on a biclique-based compressed representation that decomposes them into dense bipartite subgraphs, thereby capturing large sets of implicit edges. We first improve the iterative biclique extraction algorithm of Hern\'andez and Navarro by introducing percentile-based parameter adaptation that dynamically adjusts its parameters according to the degree distribution, enhancing both extraction efficiency and compression ratio. We then extend the Schoor multiplication algorithm to operate directly on biclique-encoded matrices, thereby enabling a compositional form of multiplication where the output can also be represented as a collection of bicliques. Our experimental results on large real-world web and social graphs show that our approach achieves substantial reductions in space and computation time with respect to CSR/CSC-based representations. For example, using biclique extraction just as a tool to speed up multiplication (but retaining the CSR/CSC format) yields up to 34-fold speedups. Further, using the biclique-based representation for input and output yields up to a 10-fold reduction in space and up to a 290-fold speedup for matrix multiplication. These results demonstrate that our representation based on bicliques is both space- and time-effective to support an algebra of Boolean matrices.
item.dc:creator: Nicol\'as Araya, Jos\'e Zagal, Cecilia Hern\'andez, Gonzalo Navarro

item.title: Learning Positive Linear Combinations of ReLUs in Fully Polynomial Time
item.description: arXiv:2610.32940v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the fundamental problem of PAC learning positive linear combinations of $k$ arbitrary ReLU activations on $\mathbb{R}^d$ with respect to the Gaussian distribution, in $L_2$ loss. We give the first fully-polynomial time algorithm for this learning task. Specifically, our algorithm draws $\mathrm{poly}(d, k, 1/\epsilon)$ samples, runs in $\mathrm{poly}(d, k, 1/\epsilon)$ time, and outputs a hypothesis that is $\epsilon$-close to the target concept with high probability. All prior algorithms for this problem require super-polynomial time in $k$ or $1/\epsilon$, or leverage strong well-conditioned assumptions on the weight matrix. On a technical level, our approach develops a novel boosting procedure of a ``weak'' learner that recovers the hidden weight vectors to constant error, in a list-decodable manner. To develop this ``weak'' learning procedure, we leverage implicit tensor computation techniques to construct a low-degree filtering procedure based on Hermite tensors of the target function. This procedure amplifies separation among (clusters of) weight vectors to learn each of them to constant error. We then argue that the same procedure can be used for improving the estimation of hidden weight vectors, using gradient descent-like updates on the Euclidean sphere. A crucial ingredient of our algorithm is a pruning approach that ensures only relevant vectors that approximate the hidden weight vectors at target accuracy are maintained by the algorithm.
item.dc:creator: Ilias Diakonikolas, Jelena Diakonikolas, Puqian Wang, Nikos Zarifis

item.title: Acyclic 2-edge-coloured graphs: polynomial-time linkages and colouring hardness
item.description: arXiv:2610.32954v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A path or cycle in a $2$-edge-coloured graph is alternating if consecutive edges have different colours. These objects are natural analogues of paths and cycles in graphs, and even more so in digraphs. A well-studied class is that of acyclic $2$-edge-coloured graphs, that is, those forbidding alternating cycles. In particular, (acyclic) $2$-edge-coloured graphs generalize directed (acyclic) graphs (DAGs), but the complexity of problems on DAGs is much better understood than that of the corresponding problems on acyclic $2$-edge-coloured graphs. We investigate the complexity of two such problems, whose directed counterparts are well-known. Our first result is an $n^{O(k)}$-time algorithm for the alternating $k$-linkage problem on acyclic $2$-edge-coloured graphs. This problem asks for $k$ vertex-disjoint alternating paths joining $k$ prescribed pairs of vertices. This generalizes the directed $k$-linkage algorithm for DAGs. For every fixed $k$, this also yields a polynomial-time algorithm for finding $k$ internally vertex-disjoint alternating $(s,t)$-paths, solving an open problem by Abouelaoualim et al. from 2008. We then consider the alternating chromatic number of $2$-edge-coloured graphs, defined as the minimum number of parts in a vertex partition such that each part induces an acyclic subgraph. This notion is analogous to the dichromatic number of digraphs, where it is known that deciding dichromatic number $2$ is NP-complete even on tournaments. Our second result is that deciding alternating chromatic number $2$ is NP-complete on complete $2$-edge-coloured graphs. Equivalently, deciding whether a graph can be partitioned into two induced threshold graphs is NP-complete.
item.dc:creator: J{\o}rgen Bang-Jensen, St\'ephane Bessy, Amadeus Reinald

item.title: Proximity Theorem and FPT Algorithm for Minimum Group-labeled Matroid Bases
item.description: arXiv:2610.32798v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Let $M$ be a matroid, let $\ell:E(M)\to G$ be a labeling of its elements by an abelian group, and let $F\subseteq G$ be finite. A base is $F$-avoiding if the label sum of its elements is not in $F$. We prove that, for arbitrary costs, a min-cost $F$-avoiding base can be obtained from any min-cost base using at most $|F|$ exchanges. This resolves the weighted proximity conjecture by H\"orsch, Imolay, Mizutani, Oki, and Schwarcz. Our main technical tool is to replace the assumption of Schrijver--Seymour Conjecture in Liu and Xu's earlier work with Kemperman--Scherk Theorem. The proximity theorem combined with approaches in earlier work gives an FPT algorithm that finds a min-cost $F$-avoiding base parameterized by $|G|$. We additionally give an FPT algorithm parameterized by $|F|$, answering a question of H\"orsch et al.
item.dc:creator: Siyue Liu, Taihei Oki, Chao Xu

item.title: Low-Crossing Spanning Paths via Quasi-Uniform Sampling and their Applications
item.description: arXiv:2610.32806v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Given a set system (X, S), we consider the problems of constructing perfect matchings and spanning paths (also known as Welzl orders) of X with low crossing numbers with respect to S. Matchings with low crossing numbers were originally introduced in the late 1980s in the seminal works of Welzl [29, 30] and Chazelle-Welzl [7], who showed that any set system (X, S) with bounded dual VC-dimension d has a matching with crossing number O |X| 1-1/d , which is optimal. Low-crossing matchings and spanning paths have found several applications outside of their initial realm of computational geometry, including algorithmic graph theory, model checking, and game theory. In many of these applications, |S| is near-linear in |X|, which motivated the search for an improved construction for this regime. However, the proposed new algorithms provided only average-case bounds or sub-optimal crossing number guarantees for d $\ge$ 2 [5, 12]. We propose a new quasi-uniform sampling based framework. This allows us to obtain a simple algorithm with expected running time of __ |X| 2 + |S| $\bullet$ |X| , which improves upon the previous-best Our result has several immediate consequences, including new faster algorithms for constructing low-crossing spanning paths for set systems induced by balls, as well as for neighborhood set systems of graphs. Moreover, we get the first quadratic-time algorithm for combinatorial discrepancy, with nearly optimal discrepancy (up to a log factor), for bounded dual VC-dimension set systems. Beyond these applications, we believe that our idea could be applied to other algorithms that use the multiplicative weight update method.
item.dc:creator: M\'onika Csik\'os (UPCit\'e), Nabil H Mustafa

item.title: Logarithmic Separation between LZ77 and LZ-End and Grammar Compression
item.description: arXiv:2610.32818v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We show that there is a logarithmic separation between LZ77 and LZ-End, and between LZ77 and grammar compression.
item.dc:creator: Philip Bille, Inge Li G{\o}rtz, Rikke Jessen, Jingxun Li, Simon Rumle Tarnow, Renfei Zhou

item.title: Exploration of Always $S$-Connected Temporal Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2602.19657v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: \emph{Temporal graphs} are a generalisation of (static) graphs, defined by a sequence of \emph{snapshots}, each a static graph defined over a common set of vertices. \emph{Exploration} problems are one of the most fundamental and most heavily studied problems on temporal graphs, asking if a set of $m$ agents can visit every vertex in the graph, with each agent only allowed to traverse a single edge per snapshot. In this paper, we introduce and study \emph{always $S$-connected} temporal graphs, a generalisation of always-connected temporal graphs where, rather than forming a single connected component in each snapshot, we have at most $\vert S \vert$ components, each defined by the connection to at least one vertex in the set $S$. We use the model of always $S$-connected temporal graphs to study \emph{subgraphs} of always-connected temporal graphs, with motivation coming from networks with a small number of ``choke-points'', such as rail networks, where all external traffic into a subnetwork comes from a limited number of external connections. We use this formulation as a tool for exploring always-connected temporal graphs admitting an \emph{$(r,b)$-division}, a partitioning of the vertex set into $r$ components, each of which is $S$-connected, where $\vert S \vert \leq b$. We show that an always $S$-connected temporal graph with $m = \vert S \vert$ and an average degree of $\Delta$ can be explored by $m$ agents in $O(n^{3/2} m^2 \Delta^{3/2}\log^{3/2}(n) + + nm^3)$ snapshots. Using this result as a subroutine, we show that any always-connected temporal graph with treewidth at most $k$ can be explored by a single agent in $O\left(n^{4/3} k^{9/2}\log^{5/2}(n)\right)$ snapshots, improving on the current state-of-the-art for small values of $k$.
item.dc:creator: Duncan Adamson, Paul G Spirakis

item.title: The Price of Universal Temporal Reachability
item.description: arXiv:2603.15176v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Dynamic networks are graphs in which edges are available only at specific time instants, modeling connections that change over time. The dynamic network creation game studies this setting as a strategic interaction where a set of $n$ vertices represents players. Players can add or remove time-labelled edges in order to minimize their personal cost. This cost has two components: a construction cost, calculated as the number of time instants during which a player maintains edges multiplied by a constant $\alpha$, and a communication cost, defined as the sum of temporal distances to all other vertices in the network. Communication occurs through temporal paths, which are sequences of adjacent edges with strictly increasing time labels and no repeated vertices. For the strict temporal shortest distance, we show a constant bound for the price of anarchy for $\alpha<2$. When $\alpha\geq\frac{1}{8}n^2$, we show Nash equilibria with a communication cost asymptotically higher than $\frac{1}{49}n^3$. We prove that the game admits a best response cycle: there exists a sequence of individually rational strategy changes that returns to the initial strategy profile without ever reaching a Nash equilibrium. This establishes that the dynamic network creation game is not a potential game and that best response dynamics may cycle indefinitely, so convergence to a Nash equilibrium or a socially optimal outcome is not guaranteed in general.
item.dc:creator: Binh-Minh Bui-Xuan, Nhat-Minh Nguyen, M\'elissa Setbel, S\'ebastien Tixeuil, Yukiko Yamauchi

item.title: Dynamic $(\Delta+1)$-Coloring Against an Adaptive Adversary: Faster, Simpler, Worst-Case, and Bounded Recourse
item.description: arXiv:2610.26182v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study fully dynamic $(\Delta+1)$-coloring against an adaptive adversary. Behnezhad, Rajaraman, and Wasim (SODA 2025) gave the first algorithm with $\tilde O(n^{8/9})$ amortized update time, later improved to $\tilde O(n^{2/3})$ by Flin and Halld\'orsson (ICALP 2025). We give a fully dynamic $(\Delta+1)$-coloring algorithm with $\tilde O(\sqrt n)$ \textbf{worst-case} update time. Unlike previous algorithms, it avoids sparse-dense decompositions and relies only on elementary data structures, resulting in a short self-contained algorithm and analysis. Moreover, it avoids global recoloring, resulting in a worst-case recourse of $3$.
item.dc:creator: Yuval Gil, Magn\'us M. Halld\'orsson

item.title: Bandits with Probing: Optimal Coverage and the Role of Feedback
item.description: arXiv:2609.15248v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In bandits with probing, a learner selects at most $k$ of $n$ arms per round, earns the largest of their rewards, and competes with the best fixed single arm. For independent arms with i.i.d. rewards in $[0,1]$ and $2\le k<n$, the minimax regret is $\Theta\bigl(\frac{n-k}{n}\min\{T,n/k\}\bigr)$, the cost of locating an unknown good arm, and observing only the maximum suffices to attain it. In particular, two probes give $\Theta(\min\{T,n\})$ regret, which resolves two open questions of Bhaskara et al. (2023) with weaker feedback. Our policy turns the probing surplus, the excess of the maximum over each probed arm, into exploration capital, and a permanent random core yields the sharp dependence on $k$. On arbitrary fixed reward arrays, same-round contrasts between blocks of arms attain the same rate, because the surplus pays for the stability of mirror descent. Winner feedback, the maximum together with its winning label, instead incurs an additional learning cost under joint i.i.d. rewards and on fixed arrays. We characterize this cost even when values are revealed only intermittently, using policies that know neither the horizon nor the revelation rate. For three independent arms and two probes, exact maxima, Bernoulli-rounded maxima with winning labels, and winning labels alone have minimax regret $\Theta(1)$, $\Theta(\sqrt T)$, and $\Theta(T)$: rounding preserves conditional means but not the rate.
item.dc:creator: Yongjie Guan
